clinicalPearls: A panniculitis produced by self-inflicted injury or the injection of foreign material into subcutaneous fat, either as a psychiatric disorder (dermatitis artefacta) or through injection of organic and inorganic substances.
Injected materials include drugs (licit and illicit), oils, milk, faeces, povidone, silicone and other foreign substances, each producing characteristic tissue reactions.
Lesions typically occur in accessible sites reachable by the dominant hand and may have bizarre, angular or geometric shapes with sharp borders unlike spontaneous panniculitides.
A discrepant or evasive history, lesions at varying stages, and failure to fit any recognised inflammatory pattern should raise suspicion.
Histology may reveal foreign material, refractile or polarisable particles, lipomembranous change, suppuration or granulomatous foreign-body reaction depending on the agent.
Polariscopy of biopsy tissue can demonstrate birefringent foreign material and is a valuable diagnostic aid.
Management combines wound care, exclusion of organic disease and infection, and sensitive psychiatric or psychological assessment and support.
Direct confrontation is usually counterproductive; a supportive, non-judgemental multidisciplinary approach is preferred.
reference.pathophysiology: Factitial panniculitis results from mechanical or chemical injury deliberately inflicted on subcutaneous fat, whether by blunt trauma, injection of exogenous substances, or introduction of infective material. The nature of the inflammatory response depends on the agent: oily and organic substances provoke a lipogranulomatous foreign-body reaction with vacuoles and giant cells, particulate or crystalline materials elicit granulomas with polarisable foreign bodies, and injected infective or irritant materials cause suppurative and necrotising panniculitis. Tissue damage releases fatty acids that amplify lobular inflammation. Underlying the physical injury is a psychological or psychiatric driver, ranging from dermatitis artefacta and factitious disorder to secondary gain, which sustains the repetitive self-injury.
additionalInvestigations: deep incisional biopsy for histopathology with polariscopy for birefringent foreign material
special stains and tissue culture to exclude superimposed infection
chemical or spectroscopic analysis of tissue for injected substances where available
imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to map injected material and deep involvement
screening for exogenous drugs or substances where injection is suspected
review of occupational and medication access and any secondary-gain context
redFlags: secondary infection, abscess or necrotising soft-tissue infection from injected material
systemic toxicity from injected substances (for example oils or drugs)
evidence of serious underlying psychiatric illness or risk of self-harm
extensive tissue destruction requiring surgical intervention
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous lesions heal with appropriate wound care once self-injury ceases, but the overall prognosis depends on the underlying psychological or psychiatric condition, and recurrence is common if this is not addressed.
pitfalls: Failing to consider a factitial cause when a panniculitis does not fit any recognised inflammatory pattern.
Omitting polariscopy and thus missing diagnostic foreign material.
Confronting the patient prematurely, which typically ruptures the therapeutic relationship.
Overlooking secondary infection introduced by the self-injury.
Treating the skin alone without engaging psychiatric or psychological services.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
management: Cessation of the self-inflicted injury or injection is the definitive step, with wound care and dressings for existing lesions
Culture-guided antimicrobials for superimposed infection and surgical debridement of suppurative or necrotic tissue where needed
Analgesia and symptomatic care for painful subcutaneous nodules
Psychiatric and psychological assessment and treatment of the underlying disorder, whether dermatitis artefacta or factitious disorder, including comorbid depression or anxiety
Non-confrontational, empathic care delivered jointly by dermatology and liaison psychiatry
Safeguarding assessment where injury is imposed on a child or vulnerable adult
Monitoring for recurrence with ongoing psychological support, as lesions relapse if the psychiatric driver is unaddressed
